title: Are We All Intelligent?
description: Taking apart the idea that intelligence means good marks: the six statements the lesson offers as definitions (school results, exams, fame, money, getting on with people, sports medals) and the answer the text gives, that being gifted is the natural birthright of almost every youngster; the three words of the same family that are never interchangeable — a gift (a noun, an ability you have), gifted (an adjective, a quality you are), a prodigy (a noun, a young person you are) — read through the story of John Adams, fluent at two, solving complex maths problems at three, the youngest pupil in Britain to pass O level maths at eight; the six types of intelligence of the questionnaire (emotional, creative, mechanical, physical, artistic, social), what each looks like in ordinary life, and the short answers it is answered with (Yes, I do / No, I don't; Yes, I can / No, I can't); writing the description of a gifted person in four moves — choose the statements, find an example for each, add age, physical appearance and social background, draft — then exchanging the draft with a partner who suggests improvements on the ideas, the grammar and the vocabulary; the acrostic poem STUDENT and its rules, before writing one on PUPILS; and the words brain, curiosity, remarkable, to undertake and to navigate
